citation: Makransky, G., & Lilleholt, L. (2018). A structural equation modeling investigation of the emotional value of immersive virtual reality in education. Educational Technology Research and Development, 66(5), 1141–1164. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9581-2
thesis: A within-subjects crossover study (N=104) comparing an immersive-HMD version of a VR biology simulation against a desktop-VR version of identical content finds immersive VR scored significantly higher on 11 of 13 measured constructs (largest effects: presence, motivation, immediacy of control, enjoyment); SEM of an a-priori CVTAE-grounded process model resolves into two parallel, non-competing paths from immersion to perceived-learning outcomes — an affective path (immersion → presence → enjoyment/motivation → outcomes) and a cognitive path (immersion → cognitive benefits → outcomes) — with presence acting as a mediator rather than a direct predictor of outcomes, contra Lee et al.'s (2010) desktop-VR finding.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Frames VR's projected educational role; argues the emotional/non-cognitive impact of immersion is under-researched relative to cognitive outcomes; states aims (A) compare emotional value of immersive vs desktop VR and (B) SEM-test the process by which immersion level affects satisfaction, perceived learning, and use-intentions.

sections.title: Existing definitions and types of VR
sections.summary: Defines VR (Burdea & Coiffet; Biocca); distinguishes CAVE, HMD, and desktop VR; adopts Cummings & Bailenson's account of immersion as an objective, system-driven property (shutting out physical reality vs offering only partial fidelity).

sections.title: Existing research about the impact of immersive VR
sections.summary: Surveys mixed prior findings — some studies (Alhalabi; Webster; Bric et al.) show immersive VR outperforming traditional/desktop instruction on cognitive outcomes; others (Moreno & Mayer 2002; Stepan et al.; Makransky et al., cited here as 2017b, cross-cluster ped-sec-10 'presence but less learning') find null/negative cognitive effects with higher cognitive load — motivating a shift toward non-cognitive/affective outcomes.

sections.title: Virtual simulations in training and education
sections.summary: Positions VR simulations as a cost-effective alternative/supplement to real-world skills training, citing meta-analytic support for simulation generally (incl. Merchant et al. 2014, cross-cluster ped-sec-16) while noting open questions specific to immersive VR's added value.

sections.title: Theory and predictions
sections.summary: Grounds the study in CVTAE (Pekrun 2000) combined with Lee et al.'s (2010) desktop-VR causal framework to build an a-priori path model: VR platform (immersive/desktop) → VR features & usability → affective variables (presence, motivation, enjoyment, control/active learning) and cognitive variables (cognitive benefits, reflective thinking) → outcomes (behavioral intention, satisfaction, perceived learning).

sections.title: Materials and Methods
sections.summary: 104 university students (39 female) used both an immersive HMD version (Samsung Gear VR/Galaxy S6) and a desktop version (laptop touchpad) of a Labster DNA-profiling crime-scene simulation, order counterbalanced, 20 min/platform, survey after each; 13 constructs measured via adapted 5-point Likert scales; CFA + paired t-tests + Mplus SEM (ordinal indicators).

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: Immersive VR scored significantly higher on 11/13 constructs; largest effect sizes for presence (d=1.67), motivation (d=1.28), immediacy of control (d=0.99), and enjoyment (d=0.94). The trimmed SEM model (CFI/TLI=0.91, RMSEA=0.06) showed presence mediating (not directly predicting) between platform/VR-features/usability and motivation/enjoyment, which predicted perceived learning, satisfaction, and behavioral intention (affective path); a parallel cognitive path ran through cognitive benefits (reflective thinking non-significant as a predictor of outcomes).

sections.title: Discussion — empirical, theoretical, practical contributions
sections.summary: Interprets the two-path model as evidence that immersion drives learning-relevant outcomes indirectly through affect (presence→enjoyment/motivation) and cognition (cognitive benefits), not directly; situates the affective path within CVTAE and flow/engagement (Csikszentmihalyi); draws design implications around usability, immediacy of control, and autonomy-supportive VR content.

sections.title: Limitations and future directions
sections.summary: Flags novelty effects (most participants were VR-naïve), reliance on self-report rather than objective learning/affect measures, small sample relative to model complexity, and unaddressed side effects such as motion sickness; calls for replication with experienced users and objective retention/transfer measures.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: 10-item scale adapted from Sutcliffe et al. 2005, operationalized per Witmer & Singer's involvement+immersion account; largest platform effect (d=1.67); mediates rather than directly predicts outcomes

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: the platform manipulation itself (immersive HMD vs desktop VR), coded as an objective system property per Cummings & Bailenson; antecedent to presence and VR features

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: operationalized as immediacy of control (4 items) and control-and-active-learning (5 items); immediacy of control shows the second-largest platform effect (d=0.99); control-and-active-learning directly predicts outcomes (β=0.23)

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: motivation (7 items) and enjoyment (3 items); largest affective-path effects (d=1.28, d=0.94); both significant SEM antecedents of perceived-learning outcomes (β=0.41, β=0.15)

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: one of two 'VR features' (3 items); platform-level antecedent to presence (β=0.21) and cognitive benefits (β=0.51)

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: not directly instrumented — only glossed in discussion via Sweller's cognitive load theory as a design risk; 'cognitive benefits' (appraisal-based) is the study's own proxy construct, not a load measure

constructs.label: situational interest
constructs.treatment: discussion-only gloss via Renninger & Hidi's four-phase interest-development theory, used to flag the novelty-effect threat to the study's own findings; not a measured construct

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: interpretive gloss only (Csikszentmihalyi 2000) on why enjoyment predicts outcomes; not instrumented

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: operationalized only as self-reported 'perceived learning' (8 items), not objective retention/transfer; flagged as the study's own limitation

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.instrument: Samsung Gear VR + Galaxy S6, stereoscopic HMD, head-tracked field of view, headset-mounted touchpad for object selection; Labster DNA-profiling crime-scene biology simulation, ≤20 min
conditions.effectDirection: significantly higher than desktop-3D on 11/13 constructs, esp. presence, motivation, immediacy of control, enjoyment

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.instrument: 15-inch laptop screen, standard touchpad input; identical Labster simulation content, ≤20 min
conditions.effectDirection: significantly lower than IVR on 11/13 constructs

conditions.label: SEM / process model (no media contrast)
conditions.design: a-priori path model trimmed via iterative CFI/TLI/RMSEA-guided modification
conditions.instrument: Mplus SEM, ordinal-indicator estimation; fit criteria CFI/TLI≥0.90, RMSEA≤0.06; final model CFI=TLI=0.91, RMSEA=0.06
conditions.effectDirection: two parallel paths (affective, cognitive) from platform to outcomes; presence mediates rather than directly predicts

readings.claim: Students prefer an immersive over a desktop VR version of a learning simulation, with the largest effects on presence, motivation, enjoyment, and immediacy of control.

Immersion affects perceived-learning outcomes indirectly, via two parallel non-competing paths — an affective path through presence/enjoyment/motivation and a cognitive path through cognitive benefits — not through a single direct effect.

Presence plays a mediating role between platform/features/usability and motivation/enjoyment; it does not directly predict the outcome variables, contrasting with Lee et al.'s (2010) desktop-VR finding that presence directly predicts perceived learning.
Reflective thinking, though strongly predicted by VR features, does not itself predict the study's outcomes and did not differ significantly between platforms.

Results likely partly reflect novelty effects since most participants had never used immersive VR before; self-report-only outcome measures and a small sample relative to model complexity further limit generalization.

interlocutors.name: Pekrun, Reinhard — control-value theory of achievement emotions
interlocutors.role: primary theoretical grounding for the affective path: enjoyment arises from appraised control + intrinsic value

interlocutors.name: Lee, Wong & Fung / Lee et al. (2010) — desktop-VR causal framework
interlocutors.role: base process-model and source of most survey items; this study extends it to add the immersive/desktop contrast and the affective/cognitive split

interlocutors.name: Witmer & Singer (cross-cluster ped-sec-02)
interlocutors.role: source of the control-factors/realism-factors account of presence that this study operationalizes as immediacy of control + representational fidelity

interlocutors.name: Dalgarno & Lee (cited as 2010; cross-cluster ped-sec-04, manifest year 2009 — citation-year discrepancy, unresolved)
interlocutors.role: cited for representational fidelity and learner interaction as key VE learning factors

interlocutors.name: Merchant et al. (cited as 2014; cross-cluster ped-sec-16, manifest year 2012 — citation-year discrepancy, unresolved)
interlocutors.role: meta-analysis cited for non-immersive VR + traditional teaching outperforming traditional-only, 2D images, or no treatment

interlocutors.name: Makransky et al. (cited as 2017b; cross-cluster ped-sec-10, manifest year 2019 — citation-year discrepancy, unresolved)
interlocutors.role: cited for the null/negative 'presence but less learning' finding with EEG-measured cognitive load, motivating this paper's affective-outcome pivot

interlocutors.name: Cummings & Bailenson
interlocutors.role: source of the objective, system-driven account of immersion; supplies the presence-meta-analysis benchmark (r=.339) this study's effect exceeds

interlocutors.name: Moreno & Mayer
interlocutors.role: source of the null-cognitive-effect immersive-vs-desktop finding (2002) and of the guided-activity design principle used in the simulation itself (2007)

interlocutors.name: Csikszentmihalyi, Mihaly
interlocutors.role: flow/engagement gloss on why enjoyment feeds the outcomes

interlocutors.name: Davis, Fred — Technology Acceptance Model
interlocutors.role: source of perceived usefulness/ease-of-use items and the behavioral-intention-predicts-use rationale

interlocutors.name: Sweller — cognitive load theory
interlocutors.role: cited briefly in discussion as the theoretical lens for the cognitive path's extraneous-processing risk; not itself instrumented

tensions.axis: presence as direct predictor of learning (Lee et al. 2010, desktop VR) vs presence as mediator only, not a direct predictor (this study, immersive+desktop)
tensions.note: The study explicitly foregrounds this contrast as an unexpected departure from the model it is built on.

tensions.axis: affective route vs cognitive route as competing explanations vs as parallel, non-exclusive paths
tensions.note: This study's own SEM treats both paths as simultaneously operative rather than resolving which one 'wins' — directly structures debate axis 4.

tensions.axis: immersion → learning as a direct cognitive effect (Alhalabi; Webster; Bric et al., cited in intro) vs immersion → learning-relevant outcomes only indirectly via affect/cognition (this study's own finding)
tensions.note: The paper's literature review stages the direct-effect optimism it then complicates with its own indirect-only SEM result — relevant to debate axis 1.

tensions.axis: novelty-driven affective gains (this study's own limitation) vs stable affective advantage of immersion
tensions.note: The authors themselves flag that most participants were VR-naïve, leaving open whether the affective-path advantage would persist with experienced users.
